newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - ABN-AMRO's MBH takeover keeps Hungary ahead.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - ABN-AMRO's MBH takeover keeps Hungary ahead.

text.p: Hungary's sale of Magyar Hitel Bank (MHB) to the Dutch ABN AMRO on Friday will keep it ahead of the pack in Central and eastern Europe as it almost completes the bank privatisation programme, analysts said.

"I see the sale as positive," said Credit Suisse First Boston's Istvan Racz. "I know of no banking systems in the region where privatisation is advanced as here and which could result in such penetration by (Western) strategic investors."
Hungary announced on Friday that it had chosen ABN AMRO as the winner of a tender to buy an 89.23 percent stake in MHB.
ABN AMRO, which will pay $89.23 million for the stake, said it planned to become one of the top three banks in the region, and would invest further $100 million in MHB over the next year.
Racz said that the privatisation of MHB, Hungary's fifth largest bank by assets, is also important for the whole banking sector and the market reforms of the country.

"In a certain sense it shows that the banking consolidation programme, which began in 1993, was not unsuccessful," he said, adding that MHB and K&H, which will be the last large bank to be privatised, were the major beneficiaries of the programme.

Hungary has spent more than 300 billion forints ($1.88 billion) in a programme which aimed at recapitalising the commercial banks and helping them to get rid of bad debts, but did not solve all the undercapitalisation problems of the bank sector.
With the sale of MHB, the commercial banks are 85 percent privatised. Only Kereskedelmi Bank Rt (K&H) and some smaller banks remained to be sold out.

Analysts said Hungary had to hurry its remaining bank sell-offs as it has undertaken to fully liberalise its banking market within the next two years in line with the requirements of the OECD, which Hungary joined in March.
The move will allow foreign banks to open branches in the country, against which Hungarian-owned banks have already proved to be less competitive, analysts warned.

"Privatisation was a positive development for the MHB (as) generally in Hungary joint venture banks have benefited the most in terms of acquiring the best business," said Agatha Pontiki of Thomson Bankwatch.
Pontiki said she expected ABN AMRO to help MHB develop its technology.
"That's where the real difference comes to providing customer services, when you have real on-line services and you can offer a great variety of complex products," she added.

Analysts said K&H bank, which the government expects to sell in 1997, needed similar support from a foreign investor, but its larger size and its less advanced reconstruction programme would make it more difficult to sell.
"K&H's network is larger and it is less integrated than MHB's," Racz said. "I still think (K&H) has a good chance to be sold next year," he added.
Racz said Austria's Creditanstalt-Bankverein, which was also a bidder for MHB, as well as other foreign banks are potential buyers for K&H. ($1=159.21 Forint)
